title: `def` defines a function, and calling it starts its execution.
body: The line `def add(a, b):` is code that declares the function. The function body does not execute immediately upon encountering that line. Actual execution begins when the function is called—for example, `add(2, 3)`—with parentheses following the function name. Beginners often assume that the `print` statement below `def` will output immediately, but the function body does not execute unless the function is called. This sidebar is intended to help you distinguish between the execution flow inside and outside a function, rather than forcing you to memorize scope as a difficult theoretical concept. When solving problems, keep in mind that a `def` line does not immediately produce an execution result, that values are passed to parameters when a function is called, and that `return` sends a value back to the caller. Even if variables have the same name inside and outside a function, don’t assume they share the same memory space; instead, follow the code line by line to see where they are created and where they are printed. `def` prepares the function, and the call initiates its execution. The body of code following `def` is not executed immediately until the function is called. When reading code, you should first read the function definition, then trace how arguments are passed at the actual call line. If a function is called multiple times, treat each call as a new execution flow.
detail: A "def" line is not a line that executes a function; rather, it prepares the function so that it can be called later. Actual execution begins on the call line, where parentheses follow the function name, as in `add(2, 3)`. When reading code, distinguish between the definition and the call, and consider that the flow within the function restarts each time it is called.

title: A parameter is the name of an input used within a function.
when_to_show: When looking at where the function call arguments go
body: In `def double(x):`, `x` is a parameter. When you call `double(4)`, the argument 4 is assigned to the parameter `x`. Inside the function, you can use 4 under the name `x`. Think of a parameter as a label that holds the input value while the function is running. It’s important to get into the habit of associating the value passed during a call with the parameter name inside the function. Rather than memorizing scope as a difficult theory, this sidebar is meant to help you distinguish between the execution flow inside and outside a function. When solving problems, keep in mind that the `def` line does not immediately produce an execution result, that values are assigned to parameters when the function is called, and that `return` sends a value back to the caller. Even if variables have the same name inside and outside a function, don’t assume they share the same memory space; instead, follow the code line by line to see where they’re created and where they’re printed. A parameter is the name used for input within a function. The arguments passed when calling a function are bound to the parameters and used within the function body. When reading code, you should first try to match the actual values on the call line with the corresponding names inside the function. If there are default values or keyword arguments, it’s a good idea to list the final values for each parameter separately.
detail: A "parameter" is the name given to an input value within a function, while an "argument" is the value actually passed when the function is called. In the case of `double(4)`, the value 4 is assigned to the parameter `x` and is used as `x` within the function body. If there are default values or keyword arguments, you should list the final values for each parameter in a table to ensure you don’t lose track of the flow.

title: The `return` statement returns a value and terminates the function's execution.
body: The `return` statement returns the function’s result to the calling location. When `return` is executed, the function’s execution ends. Therefore, even if there is code with the same indentation level below `return`, it may not be executed. `print` displays output on the screen, while `return` returns a value. When working on function problems, you need to pay attention to what value is returned and where that value is stored outside the function. This sidebar is intended to help you distinguish between the execution flow inside and outside a function, rather than forcing you to memorize complex scope theory. When solving problems, keep in mind that the `def` line does not immediately produce an execution result, that values are passed to parameters when a function is called, and that `return` sends a value back to the caller. Even if variables have the same name inside and outside a function, do not assume they occupy the same memory location; instead, follow the code line by line to see where they are created and where they are printed. A `return` statement returns a value and terminates the function’s execution. The value following the `return` is transferred to the calling location, and that result can be stored in a variable. Even if there is a `print` statement inside a function, the actual result of the call is determined by the `return` statement. When reading code, you should check under what conditions the `return` statement is encountered and how the return value is used in subsequent lines.
detail: A `return` statement returns a value created within a function to the point where it was called and terminates the function’s execution at that moment. Since the line following the `return` statement may not be executed, its position is important. Unlike `print`, it should be understood as passing a value to be used in subsequent calculations or assignments, rather than a value displayed on the screen.

title: "print" and "return" serve different purposes.
when_to_show: When You Confuse `print` and `return` Inside a Function
body: `print` and `return` serve different purposes. This card helps you distinguish between screen output and function results within a function’s scope. A `print` statement inside a function displays a value on the screen. That value does not automatically become the function’s return value. To specify a value as the function’s return value, you need to use `return`. For example, if you only use `print(3)` inside a function without a `return` statement, 3 may appear on the screen, but the return value of the function is usually `None`. Conversely, `return 3` may not appear immediately on the screen, but the calling location can receive the value and use it in other calculations. Therefore, when you see a line like `result = func()`, you must check separately what was printed inside the function and what was returned. A `def` statement does not produce an immediate result; instead, when the function is called, values are passed as parameters, and the code inside the function is executed. If both `print` and `return` are present within the same function, the value displayed on the screen, the value stored in a variable, and the function’s return value may all be different. Since function execution often ends after encountering a `return` statement, you should also verify whether the lines below the `return` are actually executed. This card encourages you to break down the execution flow rather than memorizing scope as a complex theory. When reading code, you can minimize mistakes by clearly distinguishing between the values displayed in the log, the values stored in variables, and the values returned by `return`. When practicing, create separate sections for screen output and return values for each line of function calls. When `print` is executed, write the result in the screen output column; when `return` is executed, write the value returned to the caller in the return value column. Then, check whether that value is stored in a variable or passed to another `print` statement. Doing so reduces mistakes caused by confusing the values displayed on screen with those actually stored.
detail: When reading a function, you must keep `print` and `return` separate. Write `print` in the output field, and write `return` in the field for the value returned to the caller. Even if only `print` is executed within a function, the call result may be `None`. On a line like `result = func()`, check the value displayed on the screen and the value stored in `result` separately.

title: Variables within a function are evaluated first during the function's execution.
when_to_show: 함수 안에서 새 변수가 만들어질 때
body: Variables inside a function are tracked first within the function’s execution. Rather than providing a deep theoretical explanation of scope, this card is a “Function Scope Reading Card” that tells you which lines to read and in what order when dealing with real-world problems. When you see an assignment like `total = 0` inside a function, interpret it as creating a name that is used while the function is being called and executed. Even if there is a variable with the same name outside the function, you should not assume that the assignment inside the function immediately changes the value of the outer variable. First, confirm that the `def` line defines the function’s contract—it is not a line that executes immediately. Next, at the actual call line, arguments are passed to the parameters, and the code inside the function executes from top to bottom. To determine if a value changed inside the function is returned to the outside, you must check for a `return` statement. If there is no `return` statement, the result of the call may be `None`, even if there was a screen output. When variables with the same name exist both inside and outside a function, clearly distinguish between the value outside the function before the call, the value that changes inside the function, and the value remaining after the call. When directly modifying mutable values such as lists or dictionaries inside a function, you must also distinguish whether a new name was created or whether the internal state of the passed-in object was altered. By reading in this way, even when local variables, scopes, and functions appear together, you can calmly determine which name holds meaning where. When practicing, create separate tables for outside the function and inside the function, and think of creating a new table each time the function is called. Write the actual arguments in the “parameter” column, then update the local variables from top to bottom. Finally, verify the values by dividing them into three columns: the value displayed on the screen, the returned value, and the value remaining in the outer variable. Doing this makes it less confusing to determine which scope a value belongs to, even if the names are the same.
detail: Variables inside a function are first tracked in the inner scope of the function. Even if there is a variable with the same name outside the function, you should not assume that an assignment inside the function immediately changes the value of the outer variable. It is safest to clearly distinguish between the value of the outer variable before the call, the value passed as a parameter, changes to the local variables inside the function, and the value that remains in the outer scope after the return statement.

title: Variables with the same name are treated differently depending on whether they are inner or outer variables.
when_to_show: 함수 안팎에 같은 이름이 있을 때
body: There may be an `x = 10` outside the function and an `x = 3` inside it. In this case, it’s easy to make a mistake by assuming that the `x` inside the function and the `x` outside are always the same. The `x` that is newly assigned inside the function is read first as the value used in the function’s internal flow. If you print the outer `x` after the function ends, the outer `x` may remain unchanged. This sidebar is intended to help you distinguish between the execution flow inside and outside a function, rather than forcing you to memorize scope as a difficult theory. When solving problems, keep in mind that the `def` line does not immediately produce an execution result, that values are passed to parameters when a function is called, and that `return` sends a value back to the caller. Even if variables have the same name inside and outside a function, do not assume they share the same storage space; instead, follow the code line by line to see where they are created and where they are printed. Variables with the same name inside and outside a function can behave like completely different variables. Even if you set `name = 'A'` inside a function, the `name` outside the function is not immediately changed. When reading code, you must first check which scope the current line belongs to. The more places with the same name there are, the more you need to separate their locations and the call flow to understand them.
detail: If variables with the same name exist both inside and outside a function, they can behave as if they were different variables. Even if you execute `x = 3` inside a function, the outer `x` may remain unchanged. When reading code, check which scope the current line is in, where the name was defined, and whether the output is the inner value or the outer value.

title: The result of a function call can be stored in a variable.
when_to_show: When looking at the form `result = func(...)`,
body: `result = add(2, 3)` means that the value returned by the `add` function is stored in `result`. The value calculated inside the function is returned, and that return value becomes the right-hand side of the assignment statement. Therefore, even if the name of the variable inside the function differs from the name of the `result` variable outside the function, the flow remains connected. Understanding where the result of a call goes is key to reading functions. Rather than memorizing scope as a difficult theory, this sidebar is intended to help you distinguish between the execution flow inside and outside a function. When solving problems, keep in mind that the `def` line does not immediately produce an execution result, that values are passed to parameters when a function is called, and that `return` sends the value back to the caller. Even if variables have the same name inside and outside a function, do not assume they share the same storage space; instead, follow the code line by line to see where they are created and where they are printed. The result of a function call can be stored in a variable. If written as `result = add(2, 3)`, the return value of the `add` function is assigned to `result`. Even if `print` is executed inside a function, the value that is stored is determined by the `return` statement. When reading code, you must distinguish whether the result of a call is discarded, stored in a variable, or passed on to another function.
detail: The result of a function call can be used as the value on the right-hand side of an assignment statement. In `result = add(2, 3)`, the return value of `add` is stored in `result`. Even if the variable names inside and outside the function are different, the flow is connected via the `return` statement. Distinguish whether the result of a call is discarded, stored in a variable, or passed to another function.

title: If there is no `return` statement, the result of the call may be `None`.
body: If a Python function ends without encountering a `return` statement, it usually returns `None`. Even if you use `print` inside the function, the return value may be `None` if there is no `return` statement. If you run `print(result)` after `result = hello()`, the output from inside the function and the output of `result` may appear separately. You need to distinguish between the values displayed on the screen and the results of function calls. This sidebar is intended to help you distinguish between the execution flow inside and outside a function, rather than forcing you to memorize scope as a difficult theoretical concept. When solving problems, keep in mind that the `def` line does not immediately produce an execution result, that values are passed to parameters when a function is called, and that `return` sends a value back to the caller. Even if variables have the same name inside and outside a function, do not assume they share the same memory location; instead, follow the code line by line to see where they are created and where they are printed. If there is no `return` statement, the return value may be `None`. Even if a `print` statement is executed inside a function and a value appears on the screen, the value stored in the variable may be `None` if there is no `return` statement. When reading code, you must distinguish between what a function displays and what it returns. Also note that when `None` appears in a conditional statement, it can behave like `False`.
detail: Functions that end without a `return` statement typically return `None` as the result of the call. Even if a `print` statement is executed inside a function and displays a value on the screen, the value stored in `result = func()` may be `None`. When reading code, distinguish between what a function displays and what it returns, and note that `None` can behave like `False` in conditional statements.

title: A conditional `return` statement can terminate a function early
body: If an `if` condition inside a function evaluates to `True` and the `return` statement is executed, the function terminates immediately. Subsequent `return` statements or assignments may not be executed. Therefore, in functions with multiple `return` statements, it is important to evaluate the conditions from the top down to determine which `return` statement is actually executed first. This pattern is commonly found in input validation functions. This sidebar is intended to help you distinguish between the execution flow inside and outside a function, rather than forcing you to memorize scope as a difficult theoretical concept. When solving problems, keep in mind that the `def` line does not immediately produce an execution result, that values are passed to parameters when a function is called, and that `return` sends a value back to the caller. Even if variables have the same name inside and outside a function, do not assume they share the same memory space; instead, follow the code line by line to see where they are created and where they are printed. A `return` inside a conditional statement can cause the function to terminate early. If a `return` statement is encountered inside an `if` statement, the rest of the function body may not be executed. When reading code, you should check under what conditions early termination occurs. For functions with multiple `return` statements, check the conditions from the top down and follow the return value that is actually selected.
detail: A `return` statement without a condition can terminate a function prematurely. If the `if` condition evaluates to `True` and the function encounters a `return` statement, any subsequent assignments or other `return` statements may not be executed. In a function with multiple `return` statements, the conditions are evaluated from top to bottom based on their actual values, and the function must follow the first return path that is executed.

title: If you pass a list to a function, changes made within the function may be retained.
when_to_show: When a list is appended within a function
body: If you pass a list to a function and then call `items.append('a')` within the function, the same list object is modified, so the change may be visible from outside the function as well. At the beginner level, rather than delving deeply into every concept, it’s enough to start distinguishing between values whose contents can change—like lists—and values that are calculated to produce new results—like numbers. `append` modifies the list itself. This sidebar is intended to help you distinguish between the execution flow inside and outside a function, rather than forcing you to memorize complex theories about scope. When solving problems, keep in mind that the `def` line does not immediately produce an execution result, that values are passed to parameters when a function is called, and that `return` sends a value back to the caller. Even if a variable has the same name inside and outside a function, don’t assume it always refers to the same memory location; follow the code line by line to see where it’s created and where it’s printed. If you pass a list to a function, changes made inside can affect the list outside as well. Operations that directly modify the same list object—such as `append`, `pop`, or assignment—can have lasting effects even after the function has finished executing. This is different from the flow where a new list is created and returned. When reading code, you must distinguish whether the value itself is being modified or whether a new value is being returned.
detail: If you pass a list to a function and then perform operations that modify its contents—such as `append` or `pop`—the changes may still be visible from outside the function even after it has finished executing. The behavior of directly modifying the list object differs from the behavior of creating a new list and returning it. You must distinguish between modifying the value and returning a new value.

title: Assigning a value to a numeric variable inside a function does not change its value outside the function.
when_to_show: When changing a numeric parameter inside a function
body: Even if you execute `n = n + 1` inside a function, the outer variable `x` is not automatically updated. `n` is the parameter name used inside the function, and `x` is the outer variable. For a function to pass a new value to the outside, it must return the value (e.g., `return n`), and the outside must reassign it (e.g., `x = add_one(x)`). This sidebar is intended to help you distinguish between the execution flow inside and outside a function, rather than forcing you to memorize scope as a difficult theory. When solving problems, keep in mind that the `def` line does not immediately produce an execution result, that values are passed to parameters when a function is called, and that `return` sends a value back to the caller. Even if variables have the same name inside and outside a function, do not assume they share the same storage space; instead, follow the code line by line to see where they are created and where they are printed. For numeric variables, simply assigning a value inside a function does not directly change the value outside the function. The expression `x = x + 1` inside a function should generally be interpreted as creating a new instance of `x` within the function. To modify the outer value, you may need to return the new value using `return` or use a keyword like `global`. Writing down the values before and after the call helps reduce confusion.
detail: For values such as numbers, even if you set `n = n + 1` inside a function, the outer variable `x` is not automatically updated. Parameters inside a function are tracked by their inner names first; to change the outer value, you usually need to use `return` to return a new value and then store it again. Writing the values before and after the call separately helps reduce confusion.

title: Nested functions require the inner `def` to be called as well.
when_to_show: 함수 안에 def가 또 있을 때
body: Even if there is another `def` inside a function, the inner function must be called in order to execute. When the outer function is called, the inner function definition may be set up, but unless there is a call such as `inner()`, the body of the inner function will not execute. When working on nested function problems, you must verify that there is both an outer call and an inner call. This sidebar is intended to help you distinguish between the execution flow inside and outside a function, rather than forcing you to memorize scope as a difficult theory. When solving problems, keep in mind that a `def` statement does not immediately produce an execution result, that values are passed to parameters when a function is called, and that `return` sends a value back to the caller. Even if variables have the same name inside and outside a function, do not assume they share the same memory space; instead, follow the code line by line to see where they are created and where they are printed. Nested functions require the inner `def` statement to be called separately in order to execute. Just because the outer function is executed does not mean the inner function’s body is automatically executed. When reading code, distinguish between lines where `def` prepares a function and lines where the function is actually called. It’s also helpful to check whether the inner function accesses variables from the outer function.
detail: In nested functions, the inner `def` statement merely prepares the function; its body is executed only when it is called separately. Just because the outer function is executed does not mean the inner function is automatically executed. When reading code, you should identify the outer and inner calls separately and also check whether the inner function accesses outer variables.

title: "global" indicates that the outer variable will be modified directly.
body: The `global x` keyword indicates that the function will use the outer `x` variable rather than creating a new local variable named `x` within the function. While it’s generally better to avoid using `global` in beginner-level learning, when reading code, the presence of `global` should be interpreted as a signal that assignments made within the function may affect the outer variable. For general functions, it’s safer to return values using `return`. This sidebar is intended to help you distinguish between the execution flow inside and outside a function, rather than forcing you to memorize scope as a complex theory. When solving problems, keep in mind that the `def` line does not immediately produce an execution result, that values are passed to parameters when a function is called, and that `return` sends a value back to the caller. Even if variables have the same name inside and outside a function, don’t assume they share the same storage space; instead, follow the code line by line to see where they’re created and where they’re printed. The `global` keyword indicates that the outer variable will be modified directly. Typically, assigning a value inside a function creates a local variable, but the `global` keyword allows you to assign a value to the outer variable. When reading code, check how the outer value changes after a function containing `global` is called. However, since overuse can make it difficult to trace the flow, it’s best to treat it as a warning sign.
detail: The `global` keyword indicates that the function will directly access the outer variable rather than creating a new local variable. Therefore, when a function containing `global` is called, the value of the outer variable may change. Generally, returning a value using `return` is safer, so `global` is considered a warning sign that makes it difficult to trace the flow of the program.

title: The default argument is used when no argument is provided.
when_to_show: When you see code like `def greet(name='Guest')`,
body: If a function parameter has a default value, you can omit the argument when calling the function. If you call `greet()` from `def greet(name='Guest')`, `name` becomes `Guest`; if you call `greet('Mina')`, `name` becomes `Mina`. Default values are important for determining what values are actually passed to parameters when reading a function call. Rather than memorizing scope as a difficult theory, this sidebar is intended to help you distinguish between the execution flow inside and outside a function. When solving problems, keep in mind that the `def` line does not immediately produce an execution result, that values are passed to parameters when the function is called, and that `return` sends a value back to the caller. Even if variables have the same name inside and outside a function, do not assume they share the same memory space; instead, follow the code line by line to see where they are created and where they are printed. Default arguments are used when no arguments are provided. If a function is defined as `def greet(name='guest')`, the default value is used even if `name` is omitted in the call. When reading code, you must distinguish whether a value was actually provided in the call or if the default value was used. When default values and keyword arguments appear together, it’s helpful to list the final values for each parameter in a table.
detail: The default value is the value assigned to a parameter when the argument is omitted during a function call. Even though `greet()` and `greet('Mina')` call the same function, the final value of the parameter differs. When reading code, it is helpful to clearly distinguish between the actual value provided, the default value used when the argument is omitted, and the value specified using a keyword for each function call.

title: Key-value arguments pass values by name.
body: Key-value arguments are a way of passing arguments by parameter name rather than by position. As in `greet(age=10, name='Mina')`, even if the order changes, the value is assigned to the corresponding parameter as long as the name matches. At the beginner level, when you encounter keyword arguments, simply read them by linking the parameter names in the function definition with the names in the call statement. This sidebar is intended to help you distinguish between the execution flow inside and outside a function, rather than forcing you to memorize scope as a difficult theoretical concept. When solving problems, keep in mind that the `def` line does not immediately produce an execution result; values are assigned to parameters when the function is called; and `return` sends the value back to the caller. Even if variables have the same name inside and outside a function, do not automatically assume they share the same storage space; instead, follow the code line by line to see where they are created and where they are printed. Keyword arguments pass values by name. When written as `func(age=10, name='kim')`, the name is more important than the position. When reading code, you must verify how the keywords on the calling side correspond to the parameters in the function definition. If a parameter with a default value is present, you should also check which values have been omitted.
detail: Keyword arguments pass values based on parameter names, not position. As in `func(age=10, name='kim')`, even if the order changes, the values are assigned to the corresponding parameters as long as the names match. You must map the keyword arguments in the function call to the parameter list in the function definition, and when default values are provided, you must determine which values have been omitted.

title: The function scope problem is read in four steps
body: For function problems, first check where the `def` statement is located, then find the line where the function is actually called. Second, write down how the arguments are passed to the parameters. Third, follow the local variables and the `return` statement inside the function. Fourth, verify where the return value is stored or printed outside the function. By following just these four steps, you can calmly solve most scope-related problems. This sidebar is intended to help you distinguish between the execution flow inside and outside a function, rather than forcing you to memorize scope as a difficult theory. When solving problems, keep in mind that the `def` line does not immediately produce an execution result, that values are passed to parameters when a function is called, and that `return` sends a value back to the caller. Even if variables have the same name inside and outside a function, do not assume they share the same memory space; instead, follow the code line by line to see where they are created and where they are printed. Approaching function scope problems using these four steps ensures a solid understanding. First, write down the initial values outside the function and observe how arguments are passed into the parameters when the function is called. Next, track changes to local variables inside the function, and finally, check what values remain in the outer variables after the return statement. The more variables with the same name exist both inside and outside the function, the more important this order becomes.
detail: The function scope problem can be broken down into four steps for a systematic approach. First, write down the initial values outside the function and locate the actual call line. Next, describe how the arguments are passed to the parameters, and trace the local variables and the return statement within the function. Finally, check what remains in the outer variables and in the console output after the return statement.
